scenario: Today's retrieval track asks how much to pass downstream so that it is just enough. Jina's tests find that a listwise reranker does not benefit from ever more candidates, and the stronger the first stage, the fewer candidates work best. CURATOR stops stuffing whole passages into RAG and picks the real evidence from hundreds of candidate sentences. AntEmbed and UMER both combine fast retrieval with the fine-grained judgment that reasoning brings inside one multimodal model, and UMER has the reasoning compare positives and hard negatives side by side. A medical question answering study reminds us that when a model is not accurate enough, calibration and coverage guarantees cannot produce useful answer sets.

papers.title: Too much of a good thing: Why 20 candidates beat 200 when reranking search results
papers.abstract: We expected more candidates to help, but across 25 benchmarks in Elasticsearch jina-reranker-v3.5 peaked at 100 candidates for BM25 and just 20 for semantic search, where 200 scored worse than no reranker at all.
papers.summary: Is it always better to give a reranker more candidates? Jina's team at Elastic tested its own listwise reranker on more than two dozen retrieval benchmarks, and the answer is no. With BM25 as the first stage, reranking the top 100 candidates works best, cutting about a fifth of the error on average, and adding more makes it worse. With semantic search as the first stage, the best point moves down to 20 candidates and the gain is much smaller, and sending 200 is on average worse than not reranking at all. The reason is that a listwise model reads the whole candidate list at once, so with too many candidates its attention is spread thin and noise accumulates. A model that scores candidates one by one does not have this problem, since an extra candidate never changes the order of the others. The worse the first stage, the more candidates reranking needs and the more room it has to fix things. ==Size the candidate pool by the quality of the first stage, because sending too many hurts==

papers.title: CURATOR: Scalable Fine-grained Evidence Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Decision Models
papers.authors: Shib Dasgupta, Bandish Parikh, Rashmi Gangadharaiah
papers.abstract:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides entire retrieved passages to the LLM, even though only a handful of spans within them contain the evidence pertaining to the question. While precise selection of these spans can improve context utilization, identifying them in isolation is challenging. A span may appear irrelevant by itself, and deciding whether to retain it may require examining other retrieved information.
One can evaluate each span's candidacy with the full retrieved context, but this is computationally inefficient as the same text must be processed repeatedly. Pretrained decision model can be used to efficiently evaluate multiple spans simultaneously, allowing each decision to consider the surrounding spans as well. However, our experiments show that their ability to identify relevant evidence deteriorates as the number of simultaneous decisions increases.
To address this, we introduce CURATOR, a fine-tuned decision model trained to make reliable evidence-selection decisions over large candidate sets. By training a decision model to select varying numbers of supporting spans from large candidate pools, CURATOR develops the capability to select evidence for RAG while retaining the computational efficiency of joint decision-making.
We observe that CURATOR maintains a strong evidence discrimination capability as the number of candidates increases, generalizes across different tasks and document domains, and improves downstream RAG performance, particularly when the available context is limited.
papers.summary: RAG usually stuffs whole retrieved passages into the LLM, though often only a few sentences in them can answer the question. Picking those sentences is not easy: a sentence can look irrelevant on its own, and whether to keep it may depend on other retrieved text. Judging each sentence with the full context is too expensive. Decision models can score many candidate sentences in one pass, with each judgment seeing the surrounding sentences. But the authors find that the more judgments they must make at once, the worse they get at telling useful evidence apart, and one retrieval step often brings hundreds of candidates. CURATOR trains a decision model specifically to pick a variable number of supporting sentences from a large pool while keeping the efficiency of scoring in one pass. Under a 128-token context budget, it raises evidence recall by 17.0% on average on unseen datasets and domains, and downstream answer quality by 17.4%. ==The tighter the context, the more it matters to pick the right evidence rather than add more passages==

papers.title: AntEmbed: Dual-Mode Multimodal Embedding Model for Efficient and Fine-Grained Retrieval
papers.authors: Kehang Jia, Teng Liu, Juntao Li, Hua Chen, Jinxiong Chang, Xiaobo Liang, Min Zhang
papers.abstract:
Discriminative embeddings encode original multimodal inputs efficiently but struggle with fine-grained semantics. Generative embeddings use reasoning to capture query intent and relevance evidence, but incur higher computational costs. We propose AntEmbed, a dual-mode multimodal embedding model that supports efficient retrieval and reasoning-enhanced fine-grained matching in a unified embedding space.
First, we construct retrieval-oriented reasoning content that captures query intent and confusion-aware semantic evidence. We treat original and reasoning-enhanced candidate inputs as semantically equivalent views, and use multi-positive contrastive learning with a single embedding token to align discriminative and generative embeddings.
Second, cross-mode self-distillation transfers fine-grained semantic information from reasoning-enhanced to original representations through candidate similarity-distribution distillation and query representation alignment. This strengthens discriminative embeddings without requiring additional online reasoning. Both retrieval modes share a single candidate index.
On MMEB-v2, AntEmbed-8B achieves an overall score of 81.5 with reasoning-enhanced embeddings, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.1 points.
papers.summary: Multimodal retrieval has two kinds of embeddings. Discriminative embeddings encode the raw input directly, which is fast but misses fine-grained meaning. Generative embeddings first have the model reason about the query intent and distinguishing evidence and then encode, which is more accurate but adds a reasoning pass to every query. AntEmbed, from Soochow University and Ant Group, lets one model do both while sharing a single candidate index. It treats the raw input and the input with reasoning added as two views of the same thing and pulls them into one vector space with multi-positive contrastive learning. It then distills the candidate similarity distribution from the reasoning view into the raw representation so that the non-reasoning mode gets stronger too. On MMEB-v2, AntEmbed-8B scores 81.5 overall in reasoning mode, 3.1 points above the strongest baseline. The 2B model scores 70.2 even without reasoning, beating several generative models that do reason. ==One index can choose per query between reasoning and direct retrieval==

papers.title: UMER: Unifying Embedding and Ranking via Pair-Aware Discriminative Reasoning for Universal Multimodal Retrieval
papers.authors: Libiao Chen, Xiyang Liu, Yanheng Wei, Zhenyu Tang
papers.abstract:
Modern Web information access increasingly involves heterogeneous multimodal content, including images, videos and visually rich documents. Users may seek not only globally similar content but also candidates that satisfy fine-grained attributes, relations or answer evidence under complex instructions. Supporting such access requires both efficient corpus-scale retrieval and fine-grained relevance reasoning.
Multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based embedding methods derive representations from MLLM hidden states, and recent work further uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to improve embedding capability by injecting intermediate semantic evidence into the representation. However, existing CoT methods typically use item-wise reasoning over queries and candidates in isolation, providing no explicit evidence to distinguish a positive from a semantically confusable hard negative.
Moreover, contrastive embeddings capture global similarity but struggle with meta-tasks requiring answer verification, category judgment or fine-grained reasoning. In this paper, we propose UMER, a Unified Multimodal Embedding and Ranking framework for universal multimodal retrieval. UMER replaces item-wise reflection with PairAware Discriminative Reasoning, which compares query-candidate pairs to identify instruction-relevant matching and discrepancy evidence.
UMER jointly learns contrastive embeddings for efficient global matching and discriminative ranking for explicit pairwise relevance judgment within a single MLLM. A complementary mutual distillation strategy further transfers reliable pairwise preferences between the embedding and ranking functions. On MMEB-V2, UMER-R scores 65.5/70.6 with Qwen2-VL-2B/7B, outperforming the strongest included matched-backbone baselines by 1.4/2.0 points.
UMER also supports budget-adjustable inference from efficient embedding retrieval to optional pair-aware reranking.
papers.summary: When multimodal LLMs are used for embeddings, a recent trend is to have the model write a chain of thought before encoding, injecting intermediate semantic evidence into the representation. The problem is that these chains are written for the query and the candidate separately, never seeing the hard negative that looks like the positive, so they cannot say why the positive is right or where the hard negative falls short. UMER switches to pairwise reasoning: it puts the query and candidate side by side and writes the evidence that matches the instruction and the evidence that does not. One MLLM learns both an embedding that can be indexed alone for full-corpus retrieval and a pairwise relevance judgment, and the two then distill reliable preferences into each other. In serving one can retrieve with the embedding alone and turn on pairwise reranking when the budget allows. On MMEB-V2, UMER with a Qwen2-VL-7B backbone scores 70.6, 2.0 points above the strongest baseline on the same backbone. ==To tell positives from hard negatives, reasoning has to compare them side by side==

papers.title: Calibration and Conformal Prediction for Medical Question Answering in Arabic and English: Evidence from Two Non-Parallel Benchmarks
papers.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly tested on medical exam questions, but accuracy alone does not show when an answer can be trusted. I study the calibration and uncertainty of two open-weight models, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Jais-adapted-7B-chat (both run in 4-bit precision), on 2,816 English multiple-choice questions from MedMCQA and 4,927 Arabic multiple-choice questions from MedAraBench. Accuracy was 0.561 (English) and 0.430 (Arabic) for Qwen, and 0.369 and 0.308 for Jais.
Raw option probabilities were overconfident in all four settings (expected calibration error 0.242 to 0.486), and a single temperature parameter removed 82% to 93% of that error. Split conformal prediction reached its nominal coverage in all 24 settings I tested (within 0.006), but the sets were large when accuracy was low: at 90% coverage, temperature-scaled sets contained on average 63% (Qwen, English), 78% (Qwen, Arabic), 86% (Jais, English) and 89% (Jais, Arabic) of the options.
The margin between the top two option probabilities separated correct from incorrect answers best for Qwen on English (AUROC 0.734) and worst for Jais on Arabic (0.579). Answering only the 20% most confident questions lowered Qwen's English error from 0.439 to 0.098. Jais showed a strong prior for option C (49% of English and 60% of Arabic predictions). Scoring Latin letters only cut the Arabic share to 29% but left accuracy, raw ECE and AUROC nearly unchanged.
Because the two benchmarks differ in subject, level and number of options, I do not attribute differences between languages to language itself. Code is available at 【7†this https URL†github.com】.
papers.summary: An LLM's accuracy on medical exam questions cannot say which individual answer can be trusted. The author takes two 7B open models and checks whether their option probabilities are reliable on English MedMCQA and Arabic MedAraBench multiple-choice questions. In all four combinations the raw probabilities are overconfident, and a single temperature parameter removes more than 80% of the calibration error. Conformal prediction reaches its promised coverage in every setting, but the answer sets are large when accuracy is low: to guarantee 90% coverage, Jais's sets on Arabic questions contain 89% of the options on average. Answering only the most confident fifth of questions cuts Qwen's English error from 0.439 to 0.098. The two benchmarks differ in subject and difficulty, so the author does not attribute the differences to language itself. ==When a model is not accurate enough, a coverage guarantee alone cannot yield useful answer sets==
